items.title: Sodium burns to make table salt — and then keeps wanting to react
items.claim: Sodium chloride formation looks like the textbook ionic reaction. Yet ionising Na to Na+ (+496 kJ/mol) and adding electron to Cl (-349 kJ/mol) gives a net cost of +147 kJ/mol. Why does it happen at all?
items.prompt: Where does the energy come from?

options.text: From the heat of the burning reaction
The lattice enthalpy — the enormous release of energy when Na+ and Cl- assemble into the crystal (around minus 787 kJ/mol) — dwarfs the cost of making the ions
From nowhere — the reaction is technically not spontaneous

items.reveal:
The full Born-Haber cycle for NaCl: atomise Na (+107), atomise Cl (+122), ionise Na (+496), add electron to Cl (-349), assemble lattice (-787). Net: -411 kJ/mol — exothermic and spontaneous.

Ionic bonding is NOT 'Na giving an electron to Cl' as the simple GCSE diagram suggests. It's the electrostatic stabilisation of a 3D crystal lattice. Lose the lattice (e.g., dissolve in water), and the bond is gone. NaCl(s) is stable; isolated NaCl molecules barely exist outside the gas phase.
items.why: The dot-and-cross diagram hides the energetics. Lattice enthalpy is where ionic compounds get their stability.

items.title: Chromium and copper break their own filling rules
items.claim: The Aufbau principle says fill 4s before 3d. So chromium (Z=24) should be [Ar] 4s2 3d4 and copper (Z=29) should be [Ar] 4s2 3d9. Actually they are [Ar] 4s1 3d5 and [Ar] 4s1 3d10. Two famous anomalies in introductory chemistry.
items.prompt: Why do chromium and copper 'borrow' an electron from 4s?

options.text: Quantum mechanics is approximate at the transition metals
Half-filled (3d5) and fully-filled (3d10) subshells have extra exchange-energy stability; the small 4s/3d gap is overcome by the energy gain from these stable configurations
Cr and Cu have extra protons
They are not actually anomalies — the textbook is wrong

items.reveal:
Electrons with parallel spins in different orbitals avoid each other and reduce electron-electron repulsion. A half-filled subshell maximises the count of such parallel pairs (exchange interactions), giving extra stability not captured by simple orbital-energy arguments.

For chromium, [Ar] 4s1 3d5 with six parallel-spin electrons gains more exchange energy than [Ar] 4s2 3d4. The 4s-3d gap is small, so the exchange gain wins.

Copper's [Ar] 4s1 3d10 similarly benefits from a fully-filled d shell. Further down the periodic table, niobium, molybdenum, ruthenium, rhodium, silver, platinum, gold all show similar 'anomalies' for similar reasons.
items.why: Filling rules are simplifications. Real ground-state configurations come from balancing many competing energies.

items.title: A reaction that gets cold all by itself
items.claim: Mix solid barium hydroxide octahydrate with solid ammonium thiocyanate in a beaker. The mixture turns into a slush and drops to about minus 20 degrees Celsius — cold enough to freeze the beaker to a wet wooden block.
items.prompt: How can a reaction proceed if it absorbs heat from its surroundings?

options.text: It can't — the textbook is wrong
Endothermic reactions only happen when energy is supplied externally
The enormous increase in entropy (two solids becoming liquid and gas) outweighs the unfavourable enthalpy change in the Gibbs equation
The reaction is actually exothermic at the molecular level — the cooling is an illusion

items.reveal_title: Entropy can drive a reaction uphill in enthalpy
items.reveal:
Gibbs free energy: delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. The reaction is strongly endothermic (positive delta H), but it produces 10 moles of liquid water plus 2 moles of ammonia gas from 2 moles of crystalline solid. The entropy change is huge and positive.

At room temperature T delta S is larger than delta H, so delta G is negative — the reaction is spontaneous and proceeds, sucking heat from the surroundings as it does.
items.why: Students learn 'exothermic equals spontaneous' as a rule of thumb. Entropy can outvote enthalpy when disorder rises sharply.
